english: How does one compute n! fastest?
topic: Hilbert asks how the advantages of known arithmetic formulas (summation of arithmetic series, congruence formulas, Stirling's formula) for computing specific problems can be quantified by counting elementary operations, giving the digits of π and the computation of n! as examples.

triage.modern_statement: What is the computational complexity of computing the integer n!? This can be asked in two ways. (a) Bit complexity: how many bit operations are needed to get all the decimal or binary digits of n!, measured against the cost M(N) of multiplying two N-bit integers? (b) Algebraic or straight-line complexity τ(n!): what is the fewest additions, subtractions and multiplications, starting from 1, needed to produce the number n!? This fits Hilbert's idea of counting elementary operations.
triage.answered_by: The bit-complexity version (a) was essentially settled by Peter B. Borwein in 'On the Complexity of Calculating Factorials' (J. Algorithms 6, 1985, pp. 376–380). His method uses the prime factorization of n!. Later practical refinements include P. Luschny's PrimeSwing and split-recursive algorithms. The straight-line version (b) is still open. It is tied to the Shub–Smale τ-conjecture (Smale's 4th problem) and to integer factoring (Qi Cheng, 'On the ultimate complexity of factorials', Theoret. Comput. Sci., 2004). Exact values are known only for small n (Markström, arXiv:1306.3091).

evidence.claim: Peter B. Borwein, 'On the Complexity of Calculating Factorials', J. Algorithms 6 (1985) 376–380, DOI 10.1016/0196-6774(85)90006-9.

Luschny's survey compares fast factorial algorithms. It names SplitRecursive as the fastest one that does not use prime factorization, and says the prime factorization of swing numbers is key to the PrimeSwing algorithm.

Qi Cheng, 'On the ultimate complexity of factorials' (TCS 2004), studies straight-line programs of +, −, × that compute n!. The result snippet mentions Shub and Smale's link between such programs and other complexity questions.
Markström determines the exact straight-line complexity of n! only for small n, using an exhaustive computer search of short straight-line programs.
Recent preprints still work on the Shub–Smale τ-conjecture (Smale's 4th problem) using straight-line programs.

triage.why: Hilbert's question asks how to compute n! with the fewest elementary operations. This is a real research question in computational complexity, and it is not one of his 23 problems or the 24th. The digit-level (bit-complexity) version was effectively answered by Borwein in 1985, and efficient factorial algorithms are now standard. If 'elementary operations' means ring operations on integers, the question becomes the straight-line complexity of n!. That version is still open: exact values are known only for small n (Markström 2013), and Cheng's 2004 paper studies it as a known hard problem. The Shub–Smale link is stated in the background literature rather than fully in the snippets I saw, so it rests on less direct source support. I classify it as open and known because version (b) is open and still studied. The note's wording fits either reading, so the verdict depends on interpretation. My search budget ran out before I could get the exact text of Borwein's bound or Cheng's abstract, so confidence is medium.
